Boundary smallness and harmonic weights

A bounded holomorphic function that is small on a boundary interval is small at every interior point of the same connected domain. The exponent depends on the domain and the observation point. We construct that exponent by taking an envelope of subharmonic functions, and prove that the envelope is harmonic.

Write . Let be connected and open, and let . Assume that, for some and , The domain may be unbounded or have holes. No regularity of its other boundary points is assumed. Boundary inequalities below mean limits from within .

Earlier proofs used here

  • Disk comparison and Poisson integrals, P1, proves equivalence of harmonic comparison and the circle mean inequality, and gives the positive Poisson kernel, its mass and its continuous boundary values.
  • The scalar foundation, §§12–13, proves compactness, finite derivative rules, polar calculus, geometric-series convergence and uniform convergence with derivatives. The integration foundation, §§15–16, supplies integration and differentiation under compact integrals.
  • Cauchy integrals, zeros and contour indices, CX6–CX9, proves that a holomorphic function has a smooth local power series. Thus its real Cauchy–Riemann derivatives used below exist.

In particular, an increasing bounded sequence of harmonic functions on a disk converges uniformly on its smaller concentric closed disks. Indeed apply (H3) to the nonnegative difference of two terms; their values at the center are a bounded increasing real sequence. The limit is harmonic: on any smaller circle the convergence is uniform, so passage through its Poisson integral identifies the limit with a smooth harmonic Poisson solution inside.
